utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I do understand that the translation of the transcript of the video that was played yesterday has been attached. Thank you for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it was the CV. Yes. The translation of the CV of the present witness was attached. Thank you for that, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution had a preliminary matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and good morning. It has to do with next week's schedule. For reasons which can I explain in private session should the Chamber wish, Mr. Jose Baraybar will be unable to be in The Hague next week as scheduled for his testimony. That means that the -- the schedule for next week would be RM174, followed by RM021. We are trying this morning to find an alternative witness that we could call toward the end of next week. The person that lives the closest and is most likely to be available would be Mr. John Clark, but I wanted to raise that with the Chamber and the Defence as to whether that would be a possibility. If it is, we will contact Mr. Clark this morning and see if he can come.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I spoke with Mr. Groome before this session and I informed him that for the next week we are really not flexible in any way. Because Mr. Ivetic has to undergo some surgery next week, and we cannot -- Mr. Stojanovic and I cannot cover any new witness and prepare it sufficiently for cross-examination. And also, I inform that in our schedule I cannot continue with Mr. -- he was part -- this morning as RM074. It is my witness. And I cannot continue immediately after when I finish Mr. Donia. I will have to have to some break because we anticipated that Mr. Baraybar is coming, then my witness, and then the third witness would be for Mr. Stojanovic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were -- let me see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one 174. 074, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's 174, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Lukic, Dr. Donia was scheduled to conclude his testimony today. Is there any chance that you would be able to finish his cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot promise that but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because that would perhaps create extra time for you. We could consider, for example, not to sit on Monday so as to enable you to have better time to prepare for Witness 174.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would solve the problem if I have three days in a row and I could prepare on the witness, and we can fill time next week by giving me more time for my witness. I was preparing to ask Your Honours maybe two additional hours to have eight instead of six hours. So now when we have time I think it's pretty reasonable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would then be two witnesses in four days and with some extra time for you for your witness, 174.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber is always hesitant to -- not to start hearing testimony not knowing whether at the end of the week we're short of 15 or 30 minutes. So then if we would work out a new schedule for next week, without Mr. Baraybar, then the Chamber would very much like to have a firm commitment of the parties that the programme, as then agreed upon, would -- would materialise and that we would not have a witness left over for the next weekend. If you could perhaps further discuss this with Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that the next week was scheduled short anyways. I think 14 hours, something like that. So even with Mr. Baraybar if we -- now it's -- it's, of course, open window but without Mr. Baraybar, I'm sure that we don't have to -- if we don't work on Monday we will still finish both witnesses next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you would sit together with Mr. Groome and work out a schedule to which the parties commit themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can say to the Chamber now without Mr. Baraybar there is an estimate of ten and a half hours for next week. So if Mr. Lukic is granted some additional time, it seems that it is quite certain we will finish next week, if we do not sit Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would not sit on Monday. Yes. Let's -- let's try to proceed in that way then. Then is -- could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps there's no need, but nevertheless, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, doctor.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] You were hesitant to answer in B/C/S; I saw that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we're just going to go back to a few general questions a bit. This is an area that I also found in the transcripts that I reviewed, the transcripts of your previous testimony, that is. And I noticed that you were asked to testify against an accused Serb or against -- or against an accused Croat. You never testified against a Muslim. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just -- language used. May I take it that you wanted to ask whether the witness testified in a case against an accused Serb. Testimony is not against an accused. Testimony is to tell the truth and -- may I take it that that is how you wanted to phrase --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That the case was against, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The case. That is not the same as to testify against. And I take it that your answer has to be understood in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the past, you openly expressed your views, claiming that Slobodan Milosevic was guilty of what he had been accused of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- probably so. I don't have a specific recollection of saying those words, but ... would not be surprised if I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About 50-something persons were mentioned with whom a letter was signed concerning the guilt of Slobodan Milosevic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember signing a letter. I don't -- I don't specifically recall the contents of that letter as including the conclusion that Slobodan Milosevic was guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that in previous reports you wrote about General Ratko Mladic? In the reports that were written for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you believe that General Ratko Mladic is guilty of what he stands accused of?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's not my judgement to make and would prefer not to -- I won't make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your reports or, rather, when preparing your reports, you did not talk to the main participants in what happened, Alija Izetbegovic, Ejub Ganic, Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I talked to Ganic a little bit briefly but not in great detail. But the other two persons, other than my 24 hours in court conversing with Mr. Karadzic, did not speak to him or Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, sorry to interrupt you. You referred to a letter, and the witness said he didn't remember. Do you intend to tender that letter or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's from the transcript. I don't have the actual letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the -- the question is very suggestive and nothing wrong with that. But then the Chamber, of course, would very much like to see the content of that letter, in whatever way. Unless there's any dispute about what is in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I have no idea what letter is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, if you could, in one way or another, provide the Chamber with content. If not, then, of course, the questions are without a factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to locate it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we agree that you never talked to anyone -- that you never talked to anyone who represented the ideas of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't -- I wouldn't agree to that. And I am kind of hard-pressed right now to think of who I have spoken with. I haven't, for example, interviewed anyone of that -- formally interviewed anyone of that viewpoint but I've spoken to a number of people who share it over the years.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat his question and speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to repeat your question and to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you recall a name of a member of the SDS that you talked to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different question from the one you've just asked about those who share the SDS viewpoint. But in either case, as I say, I can't recall a specific name right now, but I have heard that viewpoint expressed personally a good number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we saw that newspapers are a large share of your sources, particularly "Oslobodjenje" from Sarajevo. Would you agree with me that newspapers in Bosnia and Herzegovina were very biased, nationally coloured, before the war and particularly during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- I think most of them became nationally coloured in the course of the war. I would not agree that they were nationally coloured before the war. Some of them underwent this fairly obvious and even radical transformation on the very eve of the war, such as the newspaper "Glas" which became "Srpski Glas," and that was kind of a more, perhaps, crystal-clear instance of the change in orientation. But virtually every paper assumed some sort of colouration on the war, whether it was that of a particular ethnic group or a multi-ethnic orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that a branch, as it were, seceded from "Oslobodjenje" and an "Oslobodjenje" was founded on Serb-held territory and it is precisely because of the policy followed by "Oslobodjenje" before the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a -- a "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" formed in Pale. I think it was quite late in the war, if I'm not mistaken, maybe 1994 or something like that. But I think that a hard -- I mean, it was clear at that point that they were trying to imitate or benefit from the name "Oslobodjenje" in the Sarajevo -- the paper in Sarajevo itself. I think that given the number of Serb journalists who stayed with the "Oslobodjenje" in Sarajevo throughout the war or part of the war anyway, I would have to say I don't think that the reaction was an exclusively national one on the part of these people who founded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that "Oslobodjenje" was the official newspaper of the SDA, the party of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. It never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In "Oslobodjenje," from that time, did you ever see an affirmative article about a Serb, a favourable article about a Serb politician?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of them. And I think it's just crystal-clear from going through "Oslobodjenje" in the period particularly prior to, let's say, April 6, 1992, that the purpose of the paper, that the commitment was to give equal play to all three groups, to all three, let's say, national parties. And, in some cases, those were done through commentators. Many stories appeared in "Oslobodjenje" actually originated in "Tanjug" in Belgrade and were simply printed word for word as is often the case with wire service stories. So I don't have any problem finding many instances of "Oslobodjenje" in the pre-war period giving balanced accounts of leaders of all three groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which, of course, was not the case during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the orientation of "Oslobodjenje" shifted and shifted quite radically starting in about April 6th. But it wasn't so much anti-Serb as it was anti, let's say, SDS. It was something that was a part of the general culture in Sarajevo that was deeply opposed to the attacks and siege and favoured retaining the Sarajevo that people were used to before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every newspaper has an editorial policy as well, isn't that right, and editorial policy, as a rule, is partial, not objective. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you remember that you said, on one occasion, that you thought that there is not a single newspaper whose editorial policy is neutral and impartial?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 10 of your report in e-court, you mention Stipe Mesic. Can you tell us what the position was of Stipe Mesic, the last president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia? What was his position vis-a-vis this Yugoslavia? Did he favour the survival of that state, or, as president, did he work on breaking it up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his position was opposed to the continuation of Yugoslavia. He expressly stated, I think, in his book that he published that he -- you know, favoured destroying Yugoslavia. I don't perceive his actions in the Presidency as directed toward that goal or at least not that goal alone. He actually was -- it seems to me, trying to work out some arrangements where at least if that process were to go forward, it would do so peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Due to Mesic's views, Serbia was against him being appointed as the president of the state. However, that nevertheless happened due to pressure coming from the European community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came about as a result of an agreement that was negotiated by the European community, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: European community was of the view that Mesic had to be the president of that state; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The European community negotiators felt that the succession as it had taken place for the past decade dictated that message be confirmed in the position of the Presidency which, as you know, took place, I think, on October 8th rather than on May 15th, as it had originally happened in -- in prior years, when the Presidency -- president of the Presidency came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We now need page 10 e-court of your report, D1999 [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I said P. We don't have this many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So P1999, page 11 in English version, and page 10 in B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, you write that in the majority -- in most instances, the JNA would remain in control of contested territory or turn it over to local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where on page 7 are you reading, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should be page 11 in English version in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- page 7 of the paper. It's the first line on that page: "But in most instances, the JNA remained in control of contested territory or turned it over to local Serbs, manifesting its gradual turn toward Serb nationalism."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These territories that you call "contested" here, were these instances of the JNA seizing Croatian villages, Croatian land, and turning it over to the Serbs, or was this, in fact, Serb villages and Serb land? What do you mean by "contested territory"? And what were those instances, if you could give us some examples, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think there was a instance in which it was not the case that the JNA moved into these areas without an existing conflict breaking out between the Croatian security forces and local Serb police, or local Serb political leaders. So they were, indeed, in the first instance, acting in accord with their policy at the time, which was to separate the warring sides, separate the disputing sides. So, naturally, in a lot of cases, most cases that I know of here, the villages concerned were inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English version, on page 12 in e-court, in paragraph 3; in B/C/S version, also page 12, paragraph 3. You say in the second line of this paragraph: "On the 25th of June, 1991, assemblies of both republics simultaneously passed declarations of independence in a direct challenge to both the JNA and the federal governing bodies." In your research, did you come across any texts which claimed that these declarations were illegal and anti-constitutional?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there's a plethora of texts issued by the Presidency of -- of Yugoslavia that argued that these were unconstitutional and illegal, became sort of a fundamental theme of the Serb relationship of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro with the negotiators. And, likewise there were many tracts that argued they were fully legal and authorised by virtue of the referenda that had taken place before them. Those texts, of course, coming from the Croat and Slovene states.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the following sentence, you say: "Two days later, the JNA moved to secure Slovenia's international border-crossing points and airports ... claiming that they were under federal jurisdiction." Were these border-crossings and airport, indeed, under federal jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that -- at the end of the day, becomes a legal question and one of competing constitutional claims on the part of the Slovenes and Yugoslavia. So I -- I really would not want to try to resolve it. If you mean by that, was it under, let's say, the administration of federal authorities, I would say, yes, it was. It was under the administration of federal authority, probably border guards and things like this, that were a part of the federal security system rather than Slovene ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, an operation of Slovene forces preceded this. Slovene forces took up these border crossings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The war in Slovenia was short lived. In your research, did you come across the fact that the JNA did not even issue proper ammunition to its members?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read that allegation and have no reason to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 12 in e-court in the B/C/S version, page 13 in the English version, paragraph 1, in line 1 in the English version, you say: "In the wake of its humiliation in Slovenia, the JNA in Croatia abandoned its strategy of restraint and began to side overtly with Serb nationalists." Is it true that, at that time, there were already attacks against JNA barracks under way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The JNA did not go out of the barracks and attack anybody. Rather, they remained within the barracks and defended themselves from the barracks by opening fire on the Croatian forces who attacked the barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it's kind of a multi-faceted answer to that question. There were -- first of all, I'm trying to describe here the progression of this policy change in the late summer -- summer to late summer of 1991. The besieging of the barracks, of the JNA barracks by Croatian security forces preceded that. In the cases where they were easily taken by security -- by Croatian security force, in many cases they were, and the weapons and ammunition was then seized by Croat forces, which, in the opinion of many observers, was really what fueled their war capability in that time. The larger ones, of course, were not so much attacked as they were besieged, encircled, and just kept encircled for a period of time, rather than subject to a full-scale attack to try to conquer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you are familiar with the situation, and I'm not dissatisfied with your answer. I'm simply waiting for the interruption to conclude before putting my next question. Is it true that, in those barracks which were under siege, water and electricity supply were disconnected and they were also -- they -- the food supply was also cut off from them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interrupted intermittently, certainly, yes, and I think that's -- General Mladic himself stated those facts in -- before the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and I accept that that was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your research, did you come across the fact that the JNA gave weapons to all of those who responded to the call-up, regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think you're referring to -- well, first of all, I would want to know exactly what time-period you're talking about, if you're talking about Bosnia or Croatia, and in what time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any point in time. In 1991 and 1992. Before the war broke out in Bosnia. Did the JNA refuse to issue weapons to anyone on the basis that they were a Croat or a Muslim? Did you ever come across such a fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe the -- I mean, the JNA distributed arms in two ways. One was to those reservists who were mobilised, and those reservists who were mobilised were indeed -- included, particularly prior to late full 1991, included a good number of Croats and Muslims. It issued weapons freely to them regardless of their ethnicity or identity. The other process, though, that was going on, which was much more, let's say, discreet, was the arming of local committees of the SDS and arms that were specifically given to organised Serb entities, whether they were political -- the political party itself, or even, in some cases, the local, call them paramilitaries, or leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it comes to arming the Serbs outside of the JNA establishment, what was the purpose of that, if it was a well-known fact that anybody could respond to the mobilisation and be issued with a weapon by becoming a member of the JNA? Why would the JNA be organising distribution of weapons when anybody could receive those weapons by responding to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was part of the plan or the, let's say, wish that started, really in the -- with Belgrade authorities to provide arms to local Serb forces outside of the JNA, to strengthen their ability to resist or to actually take over areas from Croatian security forces. And eventually to fuel the Serb forces in Bosnia. So that was a very different process. The -- many local Serbs in both Croatia and Bosnia were very suspicious of the JNA and wanted it to become much more of a Serb army much faster than it did, and so that distrust caused them to want weapons of their own, apart from the JNA and that those requests were honoured and, in fact, sometimes stimulated by authorities, both within the JNA and the governments of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now page 14 in e-court, page 14 of your report, line 5 in the English version, and the first paragraph on page 14 in the B/C/S. You say that the presence of the Croat police in Kijevo and Vrlika, the two small Croat majority towns on the road between Knin and Sinj, was intolerable obstructions of the JNA's vital communications and transportation links to the south. I would like to ask you whether the mere existence of these villages was the obstacles -- obstacle or was it the barricades on the road which were, in fact, the obstacles preventing the JNA from having normal communication with other parts and other units?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both. Not a -- and I would add a third factor which was the buildup of the Croatian security forces which General Mladic reported on in his diary, and all three factors, really, were considered threats to the smooth functioning of that passageway to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you did find trace of the barricades around these two settlements on the roads around there; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I'm relying on a number of accounts in this section, including the work of Srdjan Radulovic and General Mladic himself, and, you know, other observers, and they certainly all report barricades being used, at least occasionally, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further on in e-court, on page 15 in both versions, paragraph 3 in the English and 2 in the B/C/S, you say: "The JNA took over a new role as an initiating belligerent." Would you agree that these attacks served to pull out people from the barracks under siege?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this particular one, as I understand it. I don't think there was anything under siege specifically in Kijevo, if that's what you're referring to. The -- these actions were not - at least as I can determine - designed to lift the sieges of the JNA troops that were in the urban barracks that were then under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, would you agree that in urban areas, such as the barracks in Zadar, the barracks in Split, one could not approach them if the roads were blocked and there was no possibility to free the members of the JNA who were under siege? In Zadar, for example.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the definition of "siege."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the whole issue about whether it was just the mere existence of those two villages, if I carefully read the paragraph, all the matters you asked the witness are answered in that paragraph. It is about check-points. It is about not being able to freely move. It is about the Croatian security forces. It's all explained there. And then you ask: Was it the mere existence of a village. Of course, that's not what the report says. And, again, everything you asked, all the answers given, are -- well, if not for the full 100 per cent, then at least for 80 or 90 per cent in that paragraph. So I'm just concerned about re-eliciting the same from what we read already in the report. But please proceed and keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The key issue for us was to explain the reasons for the attacks. Those were not attacks aimed at taking up territory or anything of the sort. They had a different purpose, and this is what we wanted to explain, and this is something that cannot be found in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The facts you asked for -- and you didn't ask whether this explained it. The facts you asked for are found in the report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that the military and strategic aims of the JNA coincided with the political aims of the local armed Serbs. Would you agree that there was, indeed, solely one purpose; namely, to maintain the joint state and not allow it to fall apart?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would not agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think my view on that would be the quotation that I used from General Kadijevic in describing this transition in the late summer of 1991, in which he explained the relationship between the specific JNA commitment to Yugoslavia and its transition to siding with the Serbs, with the local Serb forces. That, to me, is an extremely well expressed, very clear statement of where the JNA was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the Serbs and the JNA did not want to preserve Yugoslavia? Your answer is not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we could go to -- I can't locate it right here. But the statement of General Kadijevic, in my view, accurately captures that -- the answer to that question, and I have included it in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then in another part, you speak about the attack on Dubrovnik. What was the role of General Mladic in the attack on Dubrovnik? Did he play any role in that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You speak of combat around Vukovar. Would you also agree that General Mladic played no part in that combat either?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We went through 1991 in your report, and now, although the report is entitled: "Sarajevo" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic either is seeking contact with Mr. Stojanovic or he indicates that it would be time for the break. Perhaps it's the latter. Perhaps we should take that break then now. Yes. But, first, we'd like Mr. Donia to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break and will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, before we move on to Sarajevo, we're just going to briefly deal with the following. You also worked on other reports, not only this one about Sarajevo. In the course of your work, did you come across the following information: How did the war break out in Bosnia? What happened in Sijekovac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two different questions and may be tangentially related. But to address the second one first, in Sijekovac on, I think, the 29th of March, 1992, it might have been a day or two earlier or after, a Croatian paramilitary group crossed the Drina -- or crossed the Sava - Sijekovac is a community just across the border from Croatia - and attacked the community with -- with -- with weapons, and killed a large number of people, a significant number of people anyway, and then returned back to the -- basically devastated the village. There has been all sorts of debate since then about who exactly was targeted and who the victims were and how many of them there were. It hasn't been established to my satisfaction in anything that I have seen exactly what the motivation for that was. It's certainly known that there were local, kind of a low-level almost terrorist war going on between Serb and Croat nationalists in the region with explosions directed against particularly cultural institutions, one group of the other, and may have been an act of retaliation for that. May have been caused by other forces. But it was the -- unquestionably the Croatian paramilitary coming to this area and launching that attack that you're referring to. Now as to the second part of your question, what caused the war in Bosnia? That's -- I mean, people have written so many volumes on this topic, and it seems to me it's -- it's really hard to sort of encapsulate that in any kind of reasonably brief period of time to your answer [sic]. But I would, I guess, say generally that you had a -- one overwhelmingly large military force, overwhelming large military force in the JNA and a number of political factions seeking to mobilise their followers to promote the actual independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; whereas the political objectives of the SDS and the Serb followers of that party was to contest that and to carve out their own state and, for that purpose, they essentially mobilised or allied with the JNA, eventually assumed control of many of its units, and the hostilities reflected these things, on the military side anyway, resulted from this asymmetry of forces and the political ambitions [Realtime transcript read in error "ammunitions"] of each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. If I may interrupt you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Donia, you did say "political ambitions of each side," or did you say "ammunitions"? You are recorded as having said "ammunitions."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did say "ambitions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before this massacre in Sijekovac, were there any armed conflicts in that area at all, or was it civilians who fell victim in Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that's two questions. The -- the first part of it, were there armed conflicts in the area. There were. I would characterise the situation generally as consisting of episodic armed conflicts dating back to the fall of 1991 in Bosnia in those areas that were immediately adjacent to the Croatian war zone. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could you switch off the microphone. Mr. Mladic. Yes, and low volume. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then smaller episodes of assassinations and terrorist acts and skirmishes that seemed to have accelerated, and also barricades in various places. It kind of accelerated in the first three months of 1992. So I think you can say there -- there were, indeed, military activities and clashes going on, although not of particularly high level. And, I'm sorry, the second part of your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were civilians killed in Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, going to move on to this part where you talk about Sarajevo. That is somehow the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 21, line 2, in the English version. And that's what we need in e-court. The second paragraph on page 20 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You provide a description for this street that has east and westbound lanes and you say in its western half it was called the Street of the Proletarian Brigades and Vojvoda Putnik Street in its eastern portion closest to Marin Dvor. These streets no longer bear these names, right, the names of streets in Sarajevo were changed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Virtually every street got a new name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was done during the war, as far as back as that; right? It started then. The process was not over then.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think actually it was largely complete, at least for the centre part of the city, by 1993. There's a map from 1993 which has many of the new names on it. So -- and may have started as early as late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the names of streets that were Serb were changed; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the street names were changed. A few actually received the names of intellectual scholars, people who were Serbs, but basically all the names that had existed before, who tended to be revolutionary heros of the Second World War or period of socialism, were changed to various types of names, names sometimes after units, sometimes after individuals who were regarded highly in the history of Sarajevo, and sometimes for, you know, any other institution or purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that streets were named only after Muslims, almost?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, no, I wouldn't agree that they were named only after Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would we agree that blue boards bearing street names were replaced by green boards or plaques? Or, rather, the colour used was the colour that, in Bosnia, is affiliated with Muslim. So all of these plaques bearing street names are green, Muslim green?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, green, yes. And I would further agree that green in Bosnia and a whole bunch of other places is the colour that is used by Muslims in flags and it -- it's essentially a symbol of Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to take a brief look at page 24 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, it's the last paragraph. It is also page 24 in the B/C/S version, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say to us there that the SDA candidate Ejub Ganic came seventh in terms of the seats in the Presidency. He had identified himself as Yugoslav in the 1981 census. Ejub Ganic is one of the most extremist members of the SDA party. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would be your characterisation, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the SDA party instructed its voters that -- or, rather, to do the following: To vote for Ejub Ganic, in terms of this seventh seat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "instructed." All political -- all of the three national party formations asked their members to vote for their particular candidate for that seventh seat. So, for the Serbs, they actually nominated a Jew, Ivan Ceresnjes. I forget who the Croats nominated, but it was someone who, some way or another, met the criteria for this category of other. So the answer to your question is, yes, they did. The SDS -- SDA did request its members to vote for Ganic as the party's candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It became obvious there how this principle of one man, one vote works in Bosnia; isn't that right? One could see that the Muslims could outvote anyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina unless some other mechanisms were used to protect national interest.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This election, to me, did not make that clear, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know of this constitutional category in Bosnia-Herzegovina, constituent peoples, you read about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have this institute of protecting basic national interests; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the parliamentary -- body in parliament, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So before the war and after the war, the accepted principle was that, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there had to be some kind of control for the democratic voting based on the principle of one man, one vote. You will agree with me on that, won't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I mean, the system of selecting members of the Presidency clearly was not based on one man, one vote, and it's, I think, arguable that the elections to the Assembly were, but certainly the Presidency was already trifurcated by -- and, in fact, quadrifurcated by national affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On pages 29 through 31, you speak about different belligerent statements made by Karadzic, Koljevic, about the division of Sarajevo and the division the population. The period that you speak about here is up until the 16th of April, 1992. You will agree that, in that period, General Mladic was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To my knowledge, he was not there ever, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what was the crucial turning point that showed that the conflict would start in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know that there was one, and depending on a how one assesses these various -- the significance of these various military operations, the conflict did not start in Sarajevo. It could be said to have started in October 1991 in the village that was attacked by the JNA over the border with Croatia. Could equally be said to have started along a couple of other border incidents. Certainly could be said to have begun on the April 1st with the first incursion of paramilitaries into Bijeljina. So I -- in fact, it's not really till the 6th of April that these decisive events start to take place in Sarajevo and they are trailing a number of other events that might be said to have started the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going ask you about Sarajevo itself. You are aware of that incident or, rather, the killing that took place on the 1st of March, 1992, when the father of a bridegroom was killed at a wedding in Sarajevo. Nikola Gardovic was killed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was killed at his own son's wedding.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe a clergyman, a Serbian Orthodox priest, was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Radenko Mitrovic, a clergyman, was wounded; and Nikola Gardovic, who was killed, is also an Orthodox priest. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that Gardovic was a priest, but certainly accept that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Serb representatives in the MUP after this incident asked for the killer to be apprehended? Did you find that in various documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only MUP representatives but the political leadership of the SDS vociferously demanded that he be arrested, and in fact, I believe a warrant was put out for his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to discuss that a bit later. But do you know that "Oslobodjenje" newspaper, or, rather, Rasim Cerimagic, a journalist, wrote on the occasion of this killing: What were the members of a Serb wedding party doing in Bascarsija in the first place? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked pretty carefully at the "Oslobodjenje" coverage of that event, and it was -- it was extensive, a number of different stories over the subsequent five days. I don't specifically recall that. I have -- that statement. I have heard other Bosnian Muslims raise that question in exactly those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did find in documents that the killer was Ramiz Delalic, Celo; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he certainly was the prime suspect and was actually finally brought to court and charged with the murder in 2007. So long time between the act and his being brought to justice, but before -- I think after the very first day of the court, the trial, he was given a provisional release and was killed by an assassin, who I believe turned out to be Albanian, in a gang war dispute that had nothing to do with this original crime. So I think we can't definitively say that he was the killer, but certainly on the basis of evidence presented at that first day of trial and the assumption all along was that, yes, he was the -- he was the killer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of seeing TV programme on Sarajevo state TV, August 1992, in which Ramiz Delalic, Celo, explained how it was that he killed Nikola Gardovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen it. I know that it was admitted at the trial on that first day in 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could I ask you, we have now listened for many, many minutes to the details of the killing at the wedding party in Bascarsija. Is there any dispute about these matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one simple question, or two simple questions, could have sought the confirmation of this witness what seems not be in dispute between the parties, if it is relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this report is about the beginning of conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and we are trying to establish what was the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has told us that it didn't start in Sarajevo. And if you would have asked him -- and perhaps I could ask you now: Did it trigger further violence in Sarajevo, this killing at the wedding party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it coincided with it, because this was the last day of the referendum on independence, in which the vast majority of Croats and Muslims voted yes, and the Serbs boycotted it. And that -- the final hours of that voting seems to have been the precipitating incident for the SDS erecting barricades throughout the city and blockading -- cutting the city off from the outside and stopping traffic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it -- it certainly coincided with that, and the SDS tried to argue that this was a spontaneous response to the killings -- or the killing in Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it may be clear from this question that it is not that the Chamber is not interested in the role of that, but to go over all kind of details seems not to be -- and just out from the witness, put it to the witness, saying, Is it -- but please proceed. This case is about more than what triggered the war to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Donia, for the answer that you provided to His Honour Judge Orie. Those were the questions that we wanted to put, the setting up of the barricades and the killing of Gardovic. This man, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was the commander of the military police of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the municipality of Stari Grad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was first and foremost a gangster and really one of several very powerful and influential gangsters who took up the -- as part of their gangsterism took up the defence of the city of Sarajevo and entered into combat with the -- with the JNA and local Serb forces. Most of those appointments -- actually, a couple of them held appointments such as commander of police or something like that, and most of those were extracted from the government kind of at the -- at the point of great pressure because of the -- the advantages that that gave them in their various activities, including the -- the combat for the defence of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that this video footage was shown at trial when he spoke about the killing of Nikola Gardovic and he said that he did not hide after the killing because he actually organised the killing, together with the police in Sarajevo. He did that as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's -- what's the question? I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know of this piece of information, that he himself admitted that he organised the killing of Gardovic together with the police, or rather, with the Muslim part of the police in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- as I say, I haven't seen that video myself and I don't know exactly what he represents in that. I know that he represented that he was the killer. But beyond that, I'm not certain what he actually said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, the MUP of the Ministry of the Interior was still a joint organisation where both Serbs and Muslims, as well as Croats, worked together.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also the case, have you come across that when researching the documentation, that MUP, in fact, was the corps from which Muslim armed forces later emerged, that the Serbs joined the JNA, whereas the Muslims joined the MUP, and this is how they were predominantly armed. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be organisationally proper to say that the Territorial Defence was the core, was the basis on which the ARBiH, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was founded rather than the MUP. The MUP certainly had a role particularly after it -- after the Serbs withdrew from it on, I believe, March 30th, under the direction of the deputy minister of MUP, Momcilo Mandic. But organisationally, I think it's more the TO than the MUP that was the core of this new fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo, as a city, after the conflict broke out, split along the ethnic lines; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say it was split along ethnic lines by force. And that process was sort of -- took some time and was accompanied by varying degrees of violence. It didn't just spontaneously break into its -- into ethnic components. No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslims also violently took those parts of the city where they held majority? Is it also true that Serbs were kicked out from certain SUPs where they were a minority, in parts of town where Muslims were in majority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I receive an explanation of the use of the word "SUP" here. Certain SUPs. Or was it souks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: SUP is a smaller organisational unit of MUP. It covers usually one municipality but can cover more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- now see, yes, I was a bit confused by parts of the city and then a police structure which is -- the one is a geographical reference, the other one is an organisational reference so that confused me slightly. But if the witness has understood the question, he may answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, agree with what SUP was and the sort of local MUP junior, the local level police. I would say that's not a -- your question was not a good characterisation of what happened. I would agree that there were places in which Muslim forces dislocated Serbs, drove them out, and took control. But, really, this took place, by and large -- the exception of some overt military offensives in the western suburbs, as police stations split up and one force or the other tried to consolidate territory within the city. That was the more common problem of what you described as the ethnic division of the city and what I said was accomplished by considerable violence over a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said on page 35, English version, 37; B/C/S version 35, last line, last paragraph. You will recognise the sentence: Claiming the land on a which the Serbs lived which practically surrounded the centre of the town, the SDS created a military base for -- or, rather, created a territorial base for the military siege of Sarajevo. The fact is that the land around Sarajevo was predominantly owned by Serbs, the neighbouring, adjoining villages around Sarajevo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this sentence in your report is not true.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm -- I must say, looking at it now, my -- my modifier is not terribly clear. And when I say -- what I meant to say in this sentence is the SDS had thus established a territorial basis that nearly encircled the city centre. It wasn't the Serb-inhabited lands that nearly encircled the city centre and I, you know, regret that it is subject to that interpretation. But that was -- that was clearly not the case. As one went through these various areas, just demographically looking at them as of 1991, there were some pure Serb areas, there were some pure Muslim areas, and there were large areas which were settled by members of any and all groups in large measure because of the growth of the -- the urban growth of the city in the 1970s and 1980s, but also because of this practice of building weekend cottages which was engaged in by everybody regardless of their ethnicity. So I think that's a -- it's not the case. I know it's one of the founding myths of Bosnian Serb national belief that this -- there was a Serb encirclement of the city with Muslim -- or with Serb villages and it's just simply not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the referendum on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, the Croats and the Muslims voted for a cessation from Yugoslavia, that is to say, for independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the historical context, how do you see that? Namely, that, on the one hand, they did not wish to live with the Serbs from Serbia but they allegedly wanted to live with the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are there perhaps two kinds of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any -- any significant distinction there. The -- I mean, the voting on the 30th -- 29th and 1st was for a political option that -- you know, it was one that had been under discussion for a long time and was supported by both the national parties of the Croats and Muslims at that time. I don't think that has anything to do with the wish of those peoples to get along with and to co-operate with, to have among them, Serbs. And, in fact, I think that both the Serbs, many of whom remained in Sarajevo through the war, and the -- many of those Croats and Muslims who voted still favoured continuation of the common life of all three peoples in -- in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Naturally, we cannot speak of Sarajevo in this context alone. We have to look at the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina. On page 37, we have a title, which is quite specific. You say simultaneous desire for independence in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- simultaneous pursuit of Bosnian independence and Serb separatism, October 1991, April 1992. You basically here see this as two different things: Pursuit of Bosnian independence, on the one hand, and Serb separatism on the other hand. Why do you see it as such? Why do you not see Serbs a part of Bosnia? Why do you exclude them for opting for independent Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some -- a few did favour such independence, but I would say in -- in the main, your -- the answer to your question is -- here is that these two movements certainly interacted and in some sense reacted to the other. And then one could argue which came first and which was the initiator. But no question that the drive for independence which was sponsored by the Croat and Muslim parties, was, in substantial measure, a response to what they observed the Milosevic regime doing in trying to expand its command or control of Yugoslavia. That was long-standing. And then the, let's say, tendency of the Serbs of Bosnia, at least the political SDS portion of it, to ally with that movement was a further reason for them to consider moving toward independence. On the other hand, as they discussed and moved toward this independence, it spurred, as I indicated yesterday, it spurred the SDS to take actions to form a specifically separate Serb state on Bosnian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your report, you said that Serbs favoured status quo? Do you remember that? In the early part.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know exactly -- if you could maybe give me a page reference, I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can't find it right now. But, trust me, you did say that in the earlier stages, the Serbs favoured status quo. And the status quo presupposed remaining in the same state. It presupposed there no -- that there should be no changes and that the initiative for changes had to come from Muslim and Croats because the Serbs favoured the status quo. They did not want anything to change. Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- as a matter of reality, they did want something to change. And as they began organising this -- this -- these divisive activities in the course of, let's say, after October 15th, 1991. At one point, in an Assembly session, when they were speaking about the strategy of carving out these areas to remain in Yugoslavia, which was the ideological way that they stated this, one delegate stood up and said, Why are we withdrawing from anything? We don't have to do that. If we can favour the status quo, we do nothing at all. And of course, the leaders explained that they had to take these actions urgently in order to save the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not answer my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it possible that there's any confusion, that Mr. Lukic referred to the situation before the 15th of October, that the Serbs were happy to stay within a Yugoslavia which comprised Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in a kind of a federative situation, and what your answer is about, is the -- about the suggestion after the 15th of October and after the events of the 15th of October, where someone said, Could we not keep the status quo? And that, in that situation, the leaders explained that they could not. That's -- Mr. Lukic, have I spotted a possible source of confusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Expect the answer from me -- I'm sorry, I was more concentrated on Mr. Mladic who obviously does not feel well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and he almost fell off the chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can take a break now and see. We are a little bit early than --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Five minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Yes, a little bit early. But could you think or perhaps re-read that part of the transcript to see whether that caused the confusion. First, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed that I should inform Your Honours about the situation with the health of Mr. Mladic, and it's really bad. At this moment, he has -- everything spins. Everything is spinning. He cannot follow the trial at all. And his right hand and right leg are becoming numb and he cannot -- he couldn't walk. He just entered the courtroom with the help of guards. So I don't think that he is in a state to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were informed that the doctor has seen him and that the blood pressure was even a little bit lower than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's too low. Yes, he says it is too low for him. That's why everything is spinning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Too low for him. And that was due to loss of weight?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was informed through the communication from the UNDU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, of course, if there was a medically significant loss of weight, we would have expected it to be on the report which we received. But let me see whether we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think in the last report it was noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last report we have is from the 21st of August. And ... I don't see anything there. Which, again, is surprising, if it is significant for his present condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we have listened to what you said, and we've listened to Mr. Mladic says he feels. The simple question then is if he is unable to further continue to attend, then we would stop unless he would prefer that we would continue in his absence. I mean, it's his right to be present during trial, and we take that right seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I talk to Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mladic told me that he cannot continue and he would like -- he would like to hear the rest of the testimony of Mr. Donia -- Dr. Donia. But he cannot follow the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll have to stop. It's as simple as that. We'll ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom so that we can explain to him. Then, Mr. Lukic, that grants some extra time for you today to prepare for the next witness. The Chamber is willing, as I said before, I don't know whether you further discussed the matter with Mr. Groom, but is willing to start the next witness on Tuesday, not on Monday, and it also give you an opportunity perhaps to review your -- your -- the scheduling of your own cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there's a fair expectation then that we would finish the testimony of Dr. Donia on Monday. Unless, of course, there was any new developments. And the Chamber, of course, would like to receive a medical report on the shortest notice, that is, even if it would be delivered only during the weekend, that we are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just propose one more thing since I consulted with my colleague Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps first -- Dr. Donia, Mr. Mladic doesn't feel well. We are discussing whether or not to proceed. It looks as if we would not continue today. My first question to you would be: Are you still available on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm available Monday and Tuesday of next week. And after that, I have obligations on the other side of the Atlantic that beckon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's good to know. Mr. Lukic, you wanted to add something --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to raise one issue, yes. My colleague told me that he could, if it's possible to organise, have his witness, RM021, after Dr. Donia since we will work on Monday or, as I understand it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to switch the two witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then I have some space in between Dr. Donia and the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then, of course, we have to ask the Prosecution whether to switch Witness RM021 with Witness RM174 is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am unable to say now. We will make every effort to do that and I will notify Mr. Lukic and the Chamber within the hour whether that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and if not, of course then the Chamber will have decide on whether we would insist on starting on Tuesday the testimony of Witness 174.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It will be very hard for us. Even three days are very tight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have one day off -- of course, if we discontinue now, you would, I take it, not need the whole of the Monday but -- and, of course, the Chamber also decided that we would, anyhow, start on Tuesday with the next witness having carefully monitored the way in which you cross-examined Dr. Donia. That is one of the elements which is underlying our determination. Of course, it would be good and to be the most convenient way, if the Prosecution would be able to -- to swap Witness RM021 to 174 but there's no commitment at this moment from the Chamber that if it is not possible, that you could start any later than on Tuesday. We will adjourn for the day after Mr. Donia has been escorted out of the room. We'd like to see you back, Mr. Donia, on Monday morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have to instruct you, as I did before, not to speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether given or still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's acknowledged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we will resume on Monday, the 26th of August, at 9.30 in the morning. I don't remember whether it was in this courtroom -- I think it's in Courtroom III. Mr. Groome, you’re on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you -- your ending of the court session but I do have information on our ability to switch, and we are unable to. RM021 does not arrive until late Monday, so we would be working with RM21 on Tuesday and be prepared to call that witness on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which -- well, we have to consider that. The information is there at this moment. We'll resume on Monday, the 26th, 9.30 in the morning. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of August, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.21 p.m.,
